title: Garbo waste can
lede: Karim Rashid’s curvy polypropylene wastebasket for Umbra, one of the best-known blobjects of the late 1990s.
summary: Curvy molded polypropylene wastebasket with handle cut-outs, in bright and translucent colors. Karim Rashid for Umbra, 1995–1996.

source.label: Minneapolis Institute of Art: Garbo waste can, 2001.232

made: 1996 (Minneapolis Institute of Art and Nasjonalmuseet); the Philadelphia Museum of Art says designed 1995

evidence.note: Based on the Minneapolis Institute of Art record 2001.232 (no image published), the Nasjonalmuseet record OK-2002-0106, the Philadelphia Museum of Art record, and Metropolis (2016). No museum image of at least 800 px was inspected.

styles.note: Partial fit: a soft, curvy blobject in bright molded plastic from the Y2K period. It has no chrome or techno motifs.

context: Mia records a plastic waste can dated 1996, 33.2 × 26.7 × 25.1 cm, designed by Karim Rashid and made by Umbra, and says the “curvaceous, handled Garbo trash can is now a design icon, selling over two million units”. [Mia 2001.232](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/58170/garbo-waste-can-karim-rashid).

The Philadelphia Museum of Art gives “designed 1995”, polypropylene, translucent. [Philadelphia Museum of Art](https://philamuseum.org/collection/object/92596). Nasjonalmuseet in Oslo dates its copy 1996. [Nasjonalmuseet OK-2002-0106](https://www.nasjonalmuseet.no/en/collection/object/OK-2002-0106).

Metropolis (Misha Volf, 19 January 2016) describes an injection-molded polypropylene can released in 1996 in a “high-intensity color palette”, and says Rashid proposed in early meetings that it be translucent, “passing diffused light through its torso”. [Metropolis](https://metropolismag.com/viewpoints/karim-rashids-garbo-20/).
interpretation: Garbo is the blobject in domestic form: a cheap molded object made sensual through curves and color. It shows that the Y2K shape language reached everyday goods, not only electronics.
The shape and color are well documented, but no image was inspected, so no visual details are listed here.
borrow: Give functional openings, such as handles, soft rounded cut-outs instead of separate parts.
Let a container flare outward at the top, so the silhouette reads as a curve, not a box.
next: Find a museum image of at least 800 px (Cooper Hewitt, MoMA, or Philadelphia) and inspect it, then add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design belongs to Karim Rashid and Umbra; the Mia record marks rights as unknown.
